# Scheduled Tasks

A scheduled task is a saved prompt that fires an agent session on a recurring
schedule. Point it at an agent, a prompt, a recurrence rule, and a place to run,
and Omnigent launches that agent automatically on every occurrence — no one has
to be at the keyboard.

Scheduled tasks are managed through four built-in tools that **every agent has
automatically**. They are framework-owned and auto-registered, so an agent can
create, list, update, and delete its own recurring runs at runtime without the
agent YAML opting in. Under the hood the runner dispatches each tool to the
Omnigent server's `/v1/scheduled-tasks` REST endpoints.

## The built-in tools

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `sys_scheduled_task_create` | Create a recurring task. |
| `sys_scheduled_task_list` | List your scheduled tasks with their schedules and state. |
| `sys_scheduled_task_update` | Update a task's mutable fields. |
| `sys_scheduled_task_delete` | Delete a task so it no longer fires. |

Tasks are scoped to the calling user (or the single `local` user when auth is
disabled). You only see and manage your own tasks; a task owned by someone else
is not enumerable.

## Approval for create and update

Because a scheduled task persists work that will later run unattended, an agent
cannot save or change one silently. Every call to `sys_scheduled_task_create`
or `sys_scheduled_task_update` pauses for your interactive approval before the
task is written:

> Approve these scheduled task settings for future unattended runs?

Review the agent, prompt, host, and permission settings in that request before
accepting. The gate fires even when the call omits optional fields — inherited
defaults (for example, the host resolved at fire time or the agent's own model
and permission mode) are persisted too, so they also need your consent.
Declining denies the call and nothing is saved.

If the request selects a [permission mode that skips approval](#modes-that-skip-approval),
the prompt marks it as one, since unattended runs in that mode act without
asking. For a task that continues an existing session, the prompt also notes that
the continued session keeps its own permission mode.

This check is an always-on guard, not something you configure: it is appended
to every session's policy set — including sub-agent sessions — even when no
[policies](/docs/policies/overview) are declared anywhere, and it cannot be
removed. See [Always-on approval guards](/docs/policies/builtin#always-on-approval-guards).

`sys_scheduled_task_list` and `sys_scheduled_task_delete` do not trigger this
prompt. Tasks you create or edit directly in the [web UI](/docs/interact/web-ui#scheduled-tasks)
or through the `/v1/scheduled-tasks` REST API keep their existing authorization
rules.

## Creating a task

`sys_scheduled_task_create` takes these fields:

- **`name`** (required) — a human-readable task name, e.g. `nightly triage`.
- **`prompt`** (required) — the instruction dispatched to the agent on each firing.
- **`rrule`** (required) — the recurrence rule (see [Recurrence rules](#recurrence-rules)).
- **`agent_id`** (required) — the agent to run, e.g. `ag_abc123` (from
  `sys_agent_list` or `sys_agent_get`).
- **`execution_target`** (optional) — where each firing runs: `connected_host`
  (default) or `managed_sandbox`. See [Where a task runs](#where-a-task-runs).
- **`host_id`** (optional, `connected_host` only) — pin the run to a specific
  connected host, from the current workspace's host list. Omit to run on your
  online host at fire time; a failed run is recorded if none is online. An
  existing managed sandbox host cannot be pinned.
- **`workspace`** (optional) — its meaning depends on `execution_target`:
  - `connected_host`: an existing absolute path on the host where the fired
    session's runner starts. Requires `host_id`; omit it to start in the host's
    home directory.
  - `managed_sandbox`: a repository URL to clone into each run's sandbox,
    optionally suffixed with `#<branch>`. Omit it to use the sandbox provider's
    default.
- **`timezone`** (optional) — the IANA timezone the rule is evaluated in, e.g.
  `America/Los_Angeles`. Defaults to `UTC`.
- **`model_override`** (optional) — a per-run model override. Omit for the
  agent default.
- **`reasoning_effort`** (optional) — a per-run reasoning-effort hint, e.g.
  `high`. Omit for the agent default (the spec's
  [`executor.reasoning_effort`](/docs/build/models#reasoning-effort), or the
  harness default when the spec sets none).
- **`permission_mode`** — the permission mode for native coding agents, in the
  selected harness's vocabulary. Pass `null` for the agent default. See
  [Permission modes](#permission-modes).

Once created, the task fires automatically on its schedule until you delete it.

## Permission modes

`permission_mode` uses the selected native harness's vocabulary:

| Harness | Modes |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | Claude Code's permission modes, for example `acceptEdits` |
| Codex | `default`, `ask-for-approval`, `approve-for-me`, `full-access`, `read-only`, `bypass` |
| Cursor | `default`, `auto-review`, `plan`, `ask`, `yolo` |
| Antigravity | `default`, `skip` |
| Devin | `normal`, `accept-edits`, `smart`, `dangerous` |

Without a `permission_mode`, the task uses the agent default. For Codex that is
Codex's own default, which asks before escalations and Omnigent tool calls.
Runs are unattended, so a mode that prompts can leave a run waiting for approval.
Pick a mode that runs on its own only when its permission level suits the task.

### Modes that skip approval

These modes decide every tool call without asking anyone:

- Claude Code: `bypassPermissions`, `dontAsk`
- Codex: `full-access`, `bypass`
- Cursor: `yolo`
- Antigravity: `skip`
- Devin: `dangerous`

Use one only when the prompt and everything the run reads are trusted. A run
uses one of these modes only when the task selects it:

- **Inherited from the agent spec.** If `permission_mode` is omitted and the
  agent's spec sets a mode that skips approval, saving the task fails. Each
  firing checks again, because the agent's default can change after the task is
  saved: the run fails with error code `permission_mode_not_allowed` before it
  creates or prompts a session.
- **Continued sessions.** A task that continues an existing session
  (`session_mode: continue`) runs in that session's own mode. The firing fails
  the same way if that mode, or the agent spec's mode, skips approval and the
  task doesn't select a mode that skips approval itself. Saving likewise refuses
  a task that would continue such a session without selecting one.

The web UI offers these modes only when the server advertises
`scheduled_task_approval_skipping_modes` in `GET /v1/info`. Older servers may
refuse these modes when saving or firing, so move such tasks to another mode
before rolling back to an older server.

## Recurrence rules

The schedule is an [RFC 5545](https://icalendar.org/) `RRULE` string, evaluated
in the task's `timezone`. Examples:

```
FREQ=MINUTELY;INTERVAL=10                            # every 10 minutes (see below)
FREQ=HOURLY                                          # every hour
FREQ=DAILY;BYHOUR=9;BYMINUTE=0                       # daily at 9am
FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;BYHOUR=9;BYMINUTE=0 # weekday mornings
```

Rules are validated when you create or update a task. A rule is rejected (HTTP
400) if it has bad syntax, never fires, fires only once, or fires more often
than the minimum interval. **A task must fire at least twice**, and the minimum
gap between consecutive fires depends on where the task runs and its session
mode:

| Execution target | Session mode | Minimum interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `connected_host` | either (`new` or `continue`) | 10 minutes |
| `managed_sandbox` | `continue` (keep using the existing session) | 10 minutes |
| `managed_sandbox` | `new` (fresh sandbox session each run) | 1 hour |

Use `FREQ=MINUTELY;INTERVAL=10` for a ten-minute schedule. The shorter minimum
is allowed because connected hosts and continued sessions don't provision a new
sandbox on every fire.

The validator checks consecutive occurrences from a fixed UTC anchor, sampling
until it reaches an occurrence at least 25 hours after the first or has sampled
2,000 occurrences. Irregular recurrence sets can contain shorter gaps later, so
passing validation does not guarantee the minimum for every future firing.

An update that changes `rrule`, `execution_target`, or the session mode
revalidates the schedule against the resulting combination. For example,
switching a ten-minute sandbox task from `continue` to `new` is rejected until
the interval is at least an hour. If another change to the task's schedule,
session mode, or execution target lands while your update is being validated,
the update fails with HTTP 409 and nothing is applied. Reload the task and try
again.

Servers that accept sub-hour schedules report `scheduled_task_subhour: true` in
`GET /v1/info`. Clients connected to an older server that omits the field keep
the hourly minimum.

## Pausing, updating, and deleting

`sys_scheduled_task_update` changes only the fields you pass; the rest are left
untouched. You can update `name`, `prompt`, `rrule`, `timezone`,
`model_override`, `reasoning_effort`, `permission_mode`, `workspace`,
`host_id`, `execution_target`, and `state`.

Passing `execution_target=managed_sandbox` switches the task to a fresh sandbox
per run and clears any pinned `host_id` and `workspace`; don't set either field
in the same update. Switching back to `connected_host` leaves the task unpinned
until you set a host again.

The `state` field accepts `active` or `paused`:

- Pass `state=paused` to stop a task firing without deleting it.
- Pass `state=active` to resume it.

To remove a task permanently, use `sys_scheduled_task_delete` — deletion is not
done through `update`.

## Where a task runs

`execution_target` picks the machine each firing runs on.

### `connected_host` (default)

The task runs on one of your own connected hosts. Pin a specific host with
`host_id` (and optionally a `workspace` on it), or leave both unset and Omnigent
resolves your most-recently-active **online** host when the task fires, starting
in that host's home directory. Server-managed sandbox hosts are never picked by
this resolution, and pinning one as `host_id` is rejected — a warm sandbox from an
interactive session would leak its state into the run and break once it is gone.
If no live host can be resolved (or the pinned host is offline), the occurrence
is recorded as a failed run.

#### Random worktree

A `connected_host` task pinned to a Git repository can start each new session
in its own fresh git worktree instead of the repository directory itself. Turn
on **Random worktree** in the [web UI](/docs/interact/web-ui#scheduled-tasks),
or set `base_branch` to `HEAD` on the task through the `/v1/scheduled-tasks`
REST API (`null`, the default, runs in the selected `workspace`).

- `base_branch` requires `execution_target=connected_host` with both `host_id`
  and `workspace` set; otherwise the request is rejected.
- On each fire that starts a new session, Omnigent creates a randomly named
  `worktree-<id>` branch from that ref in a new worktree on the host, and the
  session starts there. If the host is offline the run fails with
  `host_offline`; if the worktree can't be created it fails with
  `worktree_create_failed`.
- A task that continues one session reuses that session's worktree on later
  runs. A continued session that isn't using this task's random worktree is
  rejected as incompatible.

### `managed_sandbox`

Each firing provisions a **fresh** server-managed sandbox — the same launch path
as choosing **New Sandbox** for a chat (see
[Cloud Sandbox Host](/docs/deploy/cloud-sandbox-host)). `host_id` must not be
set; a create or update that combines it with `managed_sandbox` is rejected.
The server must have managed sandboxes configured — an unconfigured server
rejects the task at create time rather than failing every fire.

To run in a specific repository, set `workspace` to a repository URL, optionally
with `#<branch>`. Each firing clones that repository into the fresh sandbox.
Leave `workspace` unset to use the sandbox provider's default workspace. Servers
that support this report `scheduled_task_sandbox_workspaces: true` in their
server info.

A sandbox created by an automation follows the server's normal sandbox
lifecycle, exactly like one created for a chat: the automation does not
override timeouts or terminate the sandbox when the run finishes. Server
operators should choose provider lifetime, idle, and cleanup settings that fit
their automation frequency and resource budget; enabling managed sandboxes
alone does not guarantee a short shutdown time.

## Starting each run from a session

Instead of a prompt alone, an automation can start every run from a copy of an
existing session. Each run then starts with that session's history.

**In the web UI**, choose **Create automation** from a session's menu in the
sidebar or in the session header. The option is offered on sessions you own when
the server advertises `scheduled_task_source_sessions` in `/v1/info`. The **New
automation** dialog shows the session under **Starts from**, and its prompt field
becomes optional **Additional instructions**. Saving copies the session, through
its last finished reply, into the automation's project.

**Over the REST API**, send `source_session_id` together with the runs'
`agent_id` to `POST /v1/scheduled-tasks`. `session_mode` must be `new`. A
`continue` task is rejected.

How these automations behave:

- **Each run starts a new session** from the copy. A run sends the automation's
  additional instructions as typed or, when there are none,
  `Perform the task from this conversation again.`, followed by the unattended-run
  note.
- **The snapshot is fixed.** Messages added to the original session after you
  save don't reach the automation.
- **Harnesses.** Runs rebuild the agent's native transcript from the copied
  messages where the harness supports it. Other native harnesses are rejected.
- **Restrictions.** A session can't be used if it is a sub-agent's session or a
  side chat, already has an automation running from it, has no agent, or has no
  finished reply yet.
- **Deleting.** Deleting a session that an automation runs from asks to **Delete
  both**. If the copy is deleted anyway, the next run fails with
  `source_session_missing`.

## How a firing runs

When a task is due, Omnigent:

1. Re-reads the task row — a task that was deleted or paused since the timer was
   armed is skipped. Under built-in accounts auth, the run also confirms the
   task's owner is still the same registered account and that the target
   `host_id` belongs to that owner; a task whose owner account has been
   removed is marked deleted and the run is recorded with error code
   `owner_deleted`.
2. Resolves the launch target for this fire only. A `connected_host` task fills
   in an unpinned host and workspace as described above; a `managed_sandbox`
   task starts hostless and binds a new sandbox in step 4. Resolved values are
   never written back to the task.
3. Creates a session bound to the task's agent, carrying the stored
   `model_override`, `reasoning_effort`, and `permission_mode` — in a fresh
   worktree when [Random worktree](#random-worktree) is on — and grants the
   task's owner ownership of the new session so the run is visible. If the
   saved permission mode can't be resolved for the agent's harness, the run
   fails with error code `permission_harness_unresolved`. If the mode isn't in
   that harness's vocabulary, the run fails with `permission_mode_unsupported`.
   In either case no session is created.
4. Launches the runner — on the resolved host, or in a freshly provisioned
   sandbox — and dispatches the prompt so the agent actually runs.
5. Records the run — stamping the task's last-run time and the run's
   conversation id.

If the latest run failed, the web UI marks the task with a **Last run failed**
warning. If that run failed before it created a session, the failure also
appears in the Inbox. See [Failed runs](/docs/interact/web-ui#failed-runs).
Clients can read the same feed from `GET /v1/scheduled-tasks/inbox`. It returns
the latest session-less failure for each of your tasks, checks up to `limit`
tasks per page (default 50, max 100), and pages with the `after` cursor taken
from `next_cursor`.

A few scheduling guarantees:

- **The database is the source of truth.** On server start, every active task is
  re-armed from the store.
- **Missed fires are not replayed.** If the server was down when a task was due,
  only the next future occurrence is armed — Omnigent does not backfill.
- **Overlapping fires are skipped.** If a task's previous run is still in flight
  when the next occurrence arrives, that occurrence is dropped.
- **Removed accounts stop firing.** When an admin
  [removes a member](/docs/collaborate/auth#removing-a-member), all of that
  user's tasks are marked deleted. A username that is later re-registered does
  not see or inherit the old account's tasks.

## Continuing in the same session

By default, every firing starts a new session (`session_mode: "new"`). With
`session_mode: "continue"`, every firing sends its prompt into one session,
which is saved as the task's `session_id`. The agent then keeps the context of
earlier runs. If you leave `session_id` unset, the first firing creates the
session and saves it on the task. In the web UI dialog, pick **Continue in the
same session** under **Session**. The option appears when the server advertises
`scheduled_task_session_modes` in `/v1/info`.

If the continued session can't take the prompt, the run fails with one of the
error codes below. Omnigent never silently starts a replacement session for one
of these:

| Situation | Run | `error_code` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The session is archived | `failed` | `continued_session_archived` |
| The owner no longer owns the session | `failed` | `continued_session_forbidden` |
| The automation has a budget, and the session already has a cost cap it did not set (for example, another automation's) | `failed` | `continued_session_budget_conflict` |

**A deleted session is replaced.** If the continued session was deleted, the
run doesn't fail. The next firing (or **Run now**) starts a new session, saves
it as the task's `session_id`, and later firings continue in it. If two firings
find the deleted session at the same time, the first one to save its new
session wins, and the other continues in that session. For a `managed_sandbox`
task, the task's sandbox is provisioned again under the same host id if no
earlier session on it is known.
